name: Brandon, Suffolk
text: Your train passes near Brandon, on the train's {side}, a Breckland town best known down the ages for its flint. Flint was mined nearby from prehistoric times, and Brandon was still a major maker of gunflints in the Napoleonic Wars; the last were made in 1945.

name: Lakenheath Fen RSPB reserve
text: Your train passes near the RSPB's Lakenheath Fen reserve, on the train's {side}, farmland until 1995 that has been turned back into reed beds and grazing marsh. Common cranes have bred here, believed to be for the first time in about 400 years.

name: St Peter's Church, Forncett
text: Your train passes near St Peter's Church at Forncett St Peter, on the train's {side}. Its Anglo-Saxon round tower, built about the year 1000, is thought one of the best in the country.

name: Rosary Cemetery, Norwich
text: Your train passes near the Rosary Cemetery, on the train's {side}, opened in 1819 by the non-conformist minister Thomas Drummond as the first non-denominational burial ground in the United Kingdom. The mustard maker Jeremiah Colman is buried here.

name: Trafford Mausoleum, Wroxham
text: Your train passes near the Trafford Mausoleum in Wroxham churchyard, on the train's {side}. Anthony Salvin designed it in the Gothic style after the death of Sigismund Trafford Southwell in 1827, and showed the design at the Royal Academy in 1830.

name: Bure Valley Railway
text: Your train passes the start of the Bure Valley Railway, on the train's {side}, a miniature railway running to Aylsham on the old trackbed of a branch line that lost its passenger trains in 1952. A footpath runs beside it.

name: Wayside cross, Norwich Road, North Walsham
text: Your train passes near the stump of a medieval stone cross by Norwich Road, on the train's {side}, one of three crosses recalling the Battle of North Walsham in 1381, the last major stand of the Peasants' Revolt. It was moved here in 1932.

name: St Nicholas Church, North Walsham
text: Your train passes near St Nicholas Church, North Walsham, on the train's {side}, one of the largest parish churches in the country. Its tower, once 147 feet to the parapet, collapsed in May 1724, and its ruin still stands 85 feet high.

name: Northrepps Aerodrome
text: Your train passes near Northrepps Aerodrome, on the train's {side}, a private airfield opened in 2007. It replaced the nearby Northrepps International Airport, whose single runway sloped so much that aircraft took off one way and landed the other, whatever the wind.

name: Cromer Hall
text: Your train passes near Cromer Hall, on the train's {side}, built in flint in 1829 to William Donthorne's design. Arthur Conan Doyle stayed in Cromer in 1901, and Baskerville Hall in The Hound of the Baskervilles can be matched to the house.

name: West Runton Mammoth
text: Your train passes near the cliffs where the West Runton Mammoth was found, on the train's {side}. After a storm in December 1990, a large bone showed at the foot of the cliffs; it turned out to be the largest nearly complete mammoth skeleton known, and the oldest found in the United Kingdom.

name: Beeston Priory
text: Your train passes near the ruins of Beeston Priory, on the train's {side}, a house of Augustinian canons founded in 1216 by Margery de Cressy. In 1317 one of its canons attacked the Bishop of Norwich with a sword; the bishop recovered, and the Pope absolved the canon.

name: Strumpshaw
text: Your train passes near Strumpshaw, on the train's {side}, on the slopes of Strumpshaw Hill, the highest land in the Broads. From the late 1790s to the mid-1810s the hill had a station of the shutter telegraph linking the Admiralty in London with Great Yarmouth.

name: St Edmund's Church, Acle
text: Your train passes near St Edmund's Church in Acle, on the train's {side}, one of Norfolk's 124 round-tower churches. The round part of its tower is the oldest part of the church, thought to be Saxon, from between 850 and 950.

name: Stracey Arms Windpump
text: Your train passes near the Stracey Arms Windpump, on the train's {side}, built in 1883 to drain the marshes into the River Bure. In the Second World War it was made into a pillbox, with gun ports in its sides; it has since been restored to working order.

name: Berney Arms Windmill
text: Your train passes near Berney Arms Windmill, on the train's {side}, the tallest drainage windmill in Norfolk. It was built in 1865 for the Reedham Cement Company, first to grind cement clinker, and has no road access even now.

name: Polkey's Mill, Reedham
text: Your train passes near Polkey's Mill, on the train's {side}, a marsh mill that worked until 1941, when a diesel pump took over. Derelict for years, it was restored to working order between 2002 and 2005.

name: Gull Wing Bridge
text: Your train passes near the Gull Wing Bridge across Lake Lothing, on the train's {side}, opened to traffic in September 2024 and the largest rolling bascule bridge in the world. A third crossing in Lowestoft was first suggested in 1918; the name came from a competition among local schools.

name: Broadhall Way
text: Your train passes near Broadhall Way, on the train's {side}, built in 1960 on the site of an old sewage works and home of Stevenage Football Club since 1980. Its record crowd of 8,040 came for an FA Cup tie against Newcastle United in 1998, with a temporary stand put up for the day.

name: Stevenage Clock Tower
text: Your train passes near the clock tower in Stevenage's Town Square, on the train's {side}. The Queen unveiled it in 1959 when she opened the first part of the new town's centre, and a bronze relief added in 1974 shows Lewis Silkin, the minister behind the New Towns Act.

name: St Martin's Church, Knebworth
text: Your train passes near St Martin's Church, Knebworth, on the train's {side}, designed by Edwin Lutyens in an Italianate style. It was consecrated unfinished in 1915 because of the First World War; its west front was added in the 1960s.

name: Digswell Viaduct
text: Your train crosses the Digswell Viaduct, whose 40 brick arches carry the line over the Mimram valley. It opened in 1850 and took about 13 million bricks, fired from clay dug on the site while it was being built.

name: Nabisco Shredded Wheat Factory
text: Your train passes near the old Shredded Wheat factory, on the train's {side}, a Welwyn Garden City landmark. Louis de Soissons, who planned the garden city, designed it after the company's factory at Niagara Falls; it closed in 2008.

name: Hatfield House
text: Your train passes near Hatfield House, on the train's {side}, built in 1611 by Robert Cecil, James I's chief minister. Part of the older royal palace still stands nearby: the childhood home of Elizabeth I, who is said to have heard she was queen under an oak on the estate.

name: Brookmans Park
text: Your train passes near Brookmans Park, on the train's {side}, a village best known for its BBC transmitting station. It takes its name from John Brokeman, who held the manor and died in 1415.

name: Wyllyotts Manor
text: Your train passes near Wyllyotts Manor, on the train's {side}, now a pub and restaurant: a late 16th-century timber barn, possibly built between 1594 and 1603, beside a house of about 1800.

name: Potters Bar Tunnel
text: Your train goes through Potters Bar Tunnel, the longest on the East Coast Main Line, beneath high ground and the M25. The first bore opened with the line in 1850; a second was not opened until 1959, and the northern end is the highest point on the line between London and Newcastle.

name: Church of St Andrew and St Mary, Watton-at-Stone
text: Your train passes near Watton-at-Stone's flint church of St Andrew and St Mary, on the train's {side}, mostly 15th century. In the summer of 1923 the young Alan Turing and his family spent six weeks with the vicar's family at the old rectory.

name: Bayfordbury Observatory
text: Your train passes near Bayfordbury Observatory, on the train's {side}, the University of Hertfordshire's observatory and one of the largest teaching observatories in the country. Its first telescope was built in 1969, and the Astronomer Royal opened it in 1970.

name: Tolmers Park
text: Your train passes near Tolmers Park, on the train's {side}, a manor house at Newgate Street. Robert Dudley, Earl of Leicester, held the manor from 1566 until his death in 1588; the present house replaced the Tudor one in the 18th century.

name: Cuffley
text: Your train passes near Cuffley, on the train's {side}, where on September 3rd 1916 the German airship SL 11 was brought down during a raid meant for London. A memorial on East Ridgeway honours William Leefe Robinson, the pilot who shot it down and won the Victoria Cross; the local football team is still nicknamed the Zeps.

name: Vicarage Road
text: Your train passes near Vicarage Road, on the train's {side}, home of Watford Football Club since 1922. When money troubles forced the club to sell the ground, fans and the former owner Elton John, who gave the takings from a concert here, helped buy it back in 2004.

name: Oxhey Chapel
text: Your train passes near Oxhey Chapel, on the train's {side}, built in 1612 by Sir James Altham for his household. In the Civil War Parliamentary soldiers used it as a store and barracks, and took lead from its roof to make musket balls.

name: Grim's Ditch
text: Your train passes near a stretch of Grim's Ditch, on the train's {side}, a bank and ditch that once ran about six miles across Harrow. Dated to the Iron Age or Roman times, it may have been a defence against the Romans or a boundary; its name comes from Grim, another name for Woden.

name: High House, Purfleet
text: Your train passes near High House in Purfleet, on the train's {side}, a farm on the hill above the Thames first built between 1552 and 1559 to divide the manor of West Thurrock between two daughters. Its dovecote, with rows of nest boxes inside, is one of the best in southern England.

name: St Clement's Church, West Thurrock
text: Your train passes near St Clement's Church, West Thurrock, on the train's {side}, on a strip of gravel by the Thames where there has been a church since before the Norman Conquest. It appears in the film Four Weddings and a Funeral.

name: Lakeside Shopping Centre
text: Your train passes near Lakeside Shopping Centre, on the train's {side}, built in an old chalk quarry. Its first shops opened in 1988, and Princess Alexandra opened it on October 25th 1990.

name: St Nicholas of Myra, South Ockendon
text: Your train passes near St Nicholas Church in South Ockendon, on the train's {side}, one of only six Essex churches with a round tower. The tower was built in the mid 13th century, and its western part fell in 1744 and had to be rebuilt.

name: State Cinema, Grays
text: Your train passes near the State Cinema in Grays, on the train's {side}, opened in 1938 with seats for 2,200. It closed as a cinema in 1988; Historic England calls it one of the best preserved of the super cinemas of the late 1930s.

name: Tilbury Fort
text: Your train passes near Tilbury Fort, on the train's {side}, which began as a blockhouse built by Henry VIII to guard the Thames. After Dutch raids it was enlarged from 1670 as a star-shaped fort with angled bastions and water-filled moats.
